content: Manages the Henley Street household and quarterly remittances
Writes letters by the carrier Thomas Hobbins
She put your father's fourteen shillings and sixpence at the whittawer's in a second ink, under the children's news, and wrote that it need not trouble you.
She meets you with the flour still on her arms, and the day was already in the letter. The opinion from London is still unsaid. The gloves wait until Saturday.
She names what money is for before she unties it, and she counts the answers she was given.
She asked once. She counted four shillings home. She did not ask again. At the door she was the whole of the seeing-off.
Her hand is steady at six days' distance, and do not come and come for harvest are one instruction.
She wrote don't come, and she also wrote come for harvest. She was told the horse was dear, and she dressed the feet.
She will strike a quantity and not say she was right, give the town's side without rescuing the sentence, count a gift as from anyone, and believe a house when one is bought.
She will not take a tidy term of years, and she will not name a house until she can turn him toward it.
At a door she asks for the back and for something said, and she will not add the house to the order.
She keeps the Michaelmas money until it falls, and she had rather he ate.
The winter wash is her decision, already paid, and the answer does not divide the money into figures.
